Conclusions

In conclusion, our work combines experimental and theoretical techniques to re-evaluate the design principles for water oxidation catalysts by unravelling the role of active sites in terms of their density,ordering and interactions between them on the reaction rate. Here we have resolved the formation of the redox centres in amorphous IrO andcrtlieIrO2as afuncion ofte poniuig timeled UV-visible spectroelectrochemistry and as a function of depth using ToF-SIMS combined with deuterium labelling. We also used DFT to provide a molecular-level interpretation of our results. From DFT, we assign the third spectral redox wave (redox transition 3) to the change

of*OHto *Oon the $\mathbf{Ir}_{\mathrm{cus}}$ site in both catalysts; in addition, the experimentally obtained $\mathbf{O}_{2}$ evolution kinetics show an exponential dependence on the coverage of the species *O, corroborating predictions from earlier DfT-based models that O-O bond formation controls the reaction rate 24-26

Our potential-decay results reveal that the intrinsic kinetics of $\mathbf{O}_{2}$ evolution, that is, the reactivity of active *O states for O-O bond formation, are comparable, or slightly faster, on amorphous IrOx compared with crystalline IrO at agiven potntial in the studied potential regime; however, the greater penetration and hence density of sites per unit geometric area of redox centres in amorphous $\mathsf{I r O}_{x}$ ,as measured using both optical spectroscopy and ToF-SIMS, account for the substantially higher geometric current density observed in this catalyst compared with crystalline $\mathrm{I r O}_{2}$ .Amorphous IrObinds more strongly $\mathrm{{\bf{t o}}^{*}O}$ than to crystalline $\mathbf{I r O}_{2}$ at low coverage; nonetheless,under the same potential for the reaction conditions, the coverage of *O is much higher than that of crystalline $\mathrm{IrO}_{2}$ , leading to greater weakening of *O as a result of repulsive adsorbate-adsorbate interactions. These two opposing effects lead to comparable intrinsic reaction rates on the two types of iridium oxide under study.
